projectDir.description: Directory holding the project, relative to the directory the CLI runs in.

version-declared.name: Ruby version is declared
version-declared.description: The project declares the Ruby version it is built and run against, and that version is no older than the configured floor.
version-declared.remediation:
Declare the interpreter where developers' shells and deploy tooling already look: a `.ruby-version` file naming the exact release, or the `Gemfile` next to your gems:

```ruby
ruby "3.3.1"
```

Without one, the interpreter is whichever Ruby the runner and the deploy image happen to have, so a syntax or standard library difference is discovered in production instead of on the laptop where it was introduced.

minVersion.description: Oldest Ruby version accepted. A declared version below this is a violation.

lockfile-committed.name: Ruby dependencies are locked
lockfile-committed.description: The project commits `Gemfile.lock`, so an install of the same commit resolves the same gem versions.
lockfile-committed.remediation:
Resolve the gems once and commit the lock file Bundler writes next to the `Gemfile`:

```bash
bundle install
git add Gemfile.lock
```

A `~>` or `>=` requirement resolves to whatever RubyGems serves that day, so an application without a lock file resolves differently on every deploy, and the gems that shipped are not the gems that were reviewed.

single-gem-source.name: Gems come from one trusted source
single-gem-source.description: The `Gemfile` resolves gems from at most one source, and that source is one the repository trusts. The `Gemfile` is Ruby code, not a declaration, so it is read by pattern. A second source that is found is a real finding, but finding only one doesn't prove there is only one: a source named inside a condition, a loop or an `eval` isn't detected.
single-gem-source.remediation:
Keep one `source` line at the top of the `Gemfile`, and name any other source only on the gems that need it:

```ruby
source "https://rubygems.org"

gem "company-internal", source: "https://gems.internal.example.com"
```

With two sources for the whole `Gemfile`, Bundler resolves each gem from whichever source offers the higher version. Anyone who can publish `company-internal` to the public index can then take over the install without touching this repository. This is exactly what a dependency confusion attack relies on.

allowedSources.description: Comma separated gem sources the repository trusts. A source not on this list is a violation. Trailing slashes and letter case are ignored when comparing.

no-git-dependencies.name: No gem is fetched from git
no-git-dependencies.description: No gem the manifests declare is fetched from a git repository instead of a gem source. The `Gemfile` is Ruby code, not a declaration, so it is read by pattern. A git gem that is found is a real finding, but finding none doesn't prove there are none: a gem added inside a condition, a loop or an `eval` isn't detected.
no-git-dependencies.remediation:
Depend on a published release from the same source as the rest of the build:

```ruby
gem "company-widget", "~> 2.1"
```

If a fork is the only place the fix exists, publish that fork as a gem instead of pointing the build at a branch. A `git:` or `github:` gem is fetched from a repository someone can force push, rename or make private. An update can then install code no index ever published, and a build that worked yesterday can stop resolving entirely.
